title: AWS CWI Exam Prep in Minneapolis, MN: 6-Day Course
description: Six-day AWS CWI exam prep for Twin Cities welders: cold-weather metallurgy, MnDOT bridge steel, refinery piping and the nearest Part B sites. Get a quote.
h1: AWS CWI Exam Prep in Minneapolis and St. Paul: Six Days to Get Ready for the Certified Welding Inspector Exam
html:
Welding inspectors in Minneapolis and St. Paul work in a climate that tests both people and steel. Field welds go down in January wind, bridge girders are ordered with toughness for deep cold, and the region's factories turn out heavy equipment that has to survive the same winters. If you are a welder, fitter, quality technician, NDT technician or engineer in the Twin Cities aiming at the AWS Certified Welding Inspector credential, Atlantis NDT can prepare you with a six-day (6-day) exam-prep course, taken online on your own schedule or brought to your employer's plant for a group. AWS sets the eligibility rules, runs every part of the examination and awards the certification; Atlantis's job is to get you ready to pass it. Ask for a Minneapolis quote when you know roughly when you want to sit.

The Twin Cities welding economy in brief

Minneapolis is better known for finance, retail and medical technology than for heavy industry, but the metro area and the state around it carry a substantial welding workload. Manufacturers headquartered or operating here build recreational vehicles, outdoor power equipment, pumps and fluid-handling systems, agricultural and food-processing machinery, and truck bodies. Structural steel fabricators supply downtown towers, stadiums, hospitals and warehouse construction. Two oil refineries operate in the south-east metro, and the state is crossed by crude oil, refined product and natural gas pipelines. North of the metro, the taconite mines of the Iron Range run fleets of large equipment that need repair welding year round.

Each of those sectors hires or contracts welding inspectors for different reasons. A fabricator certified to a customer's quality program needs someone in-house who can sign weld inspection records. A general contractor on a large building needs third-party inspection of structural welds to satisfy the engineer of record. A refinery turnaround needs inspectors who understand piping codes. A pipeline spread needs inspectors who know API 1104. The CWI credential is the common currency across all of them, which is why it travels well between employers in a region with this mix.

Welding in the cold: Part A metallurgy you will use every winter

Much of the Fundamentals part of the exam is metallurgy, and in Minnesota that material is not abstract. Cold, damp steel is where hydrogen-induced cracking starts. Moisture on the joint, in the flux or in the air supplies hydrogen to the weld; fast cooling of a cold, thick plate produces hard microstructures in the heat-affected zone; and restraint in a stiff connection adds the stress. Remove any one of the three and the risk falls. That is why preheat, low-hydrogen consumables, electrode storage ovens and slow cooling all show up as inspection hold points rather than optional good practice.

AWS D1.1 builds that thinking into its rules. Its preheat requirements rise with steel strength and thickness, it places a lower limit on the ambient temperature for welding, and it requires base metal below freezing to be warmed before welding even where its preheat table would otherwise ask for nothing. Contractors here routinely tent and heat connections in winter, and the welding inspector is the person who checks that a temperature crayon or contact thermometer reading was taken at the right distance from the joint and at the right time, not just once at the start of the shift.

Toughness is the other cold-weather topic. Bridge steels and filler metals are ordered with Charpy V-notch impact requirements tied to the lowest service temperature the structure is expected to see, and an inspector reviewing mill certificates and filler metal certifications has to confirm those values were met. The Charpy test, what it measures and why it is run cold are standard Fundamentals content, and Minnesota candidates have more reason than most to understand it properly.

Bridges, MnDOT and what Minnesota took from 2007

Every bridge professional in the state remembers the 2007 collapse of the I-35W bridge over the Mississippi in Minneapolis. The National Transportation Safety Board traced it to gusset plates that were undersized in the original design, not to welding, but the disaster changed how closely Minnesota and the rest of the country look at steel bridges, their connections and their load ratings. The Minnesota Department of Transportation and county and city bridge owners maintain thousands of structures, and rehabilitation, strengthening and replacement work keeps steel fabricators and field inspectors busy.

For new girders and floor-system steel the governing document is AWS D1.5, the Bridge Welding Code, and it is one of the books AWS will let you take into Part C. D1.5 is stricter than the structural code in several ways: it limits processes and procedures more tightly, carries extra provisions for fracture-critical members whose failure could bring a span down, and asks more of qualification testing. A candidate who works at a bridge fabrication shop, or who inspects bridge steel for a consultant, should prepare with D1.5 rather than D1.1. The D1.5 summary and the article on NDT for bridges under AASHTO give useful background.

Equipment builders, job shops and robot cells

Much of the region's welding happens indoors, on production lines and in job shops making frames, booms, tanks, chassis and weldments for machinery. A lot of it is robotic. Inspection in that setting is less about one large connection and more about consistency: verifying that a robot program still produces the specified fillet size after a fixture change, catching undercut or incomplete fusion trends before a batch ships, and checking that the welding procedure posted at the cell actually covers the material and thickness on the fixture.

Machinery welding is often governed by a customer specification or an internal standard rather than a building code, but those documents usually borrow their structure and acceptance criteria from AWS D1.1, so D1.1 remains the natural Part C choice for most production inspectors. Many shops also run magnetic particle testing on critical welds; see magnetic particle testing in fabrication for how that method sits alongside visual weld inspection. Understanding how procedures and welder tests relate is covered in the WPS, PQR and WPQ guide.

Refineries, pipelines and power: when the piping codes apply

The two refineries south-east of St. Paul hold maintenance turnarounds and capital projects that bring in welders, pipefitters and inspectors by the hundred. Process piping in a refinery is built and repaired to ASME B31.3, which AWS offers as a Part C book in its 2024 edition. Generating stations use ASME B31.1, also on the list. If your career is heading toward plant work, studying the piping code you will use is a sound choice; the B31.3 overview explains its structure, and ultrasonic testing in refining covers the NDT that refinery welds usually receive.

Pipeline construction and replacement projects across Minnesota follow API 1104, the pipeline welding standard, offered by AWS in its 22nd edition. Pipeline inspectors working on construction spreads deal with field girth welds, weather, mainline crews moving fast, and the radiographic or ultrasonic results that follow the welders. A CWI with API 1104 as the Part C code is well placed for that work; see the API 1104 summary. A welding inspector on a refinery job sometimes meets API inspector roles too. Those are separate credentials with separate exams; this side-by-side look at three inspection credentials explains where each one applies. Atlantis does not prepare candidates for API inspector exams.

Food plants and stainless sanitary work

Minnesota's farm economy feeds a large food and dairy processing sector, and those plants install and modify stainless steel process lines constantly. Sanitary tubing is usually orbital or manual gas tungsten arc welded with an internal purge, and the inspection questions are about root profile, discoloration inside the tube, alignment and cleanliness. That work sits close to the piping codes and to owner sanitary standards. CWI candidates from food plant maintenance or contract fabrication often choose B31.3 for Part C. For the penetrant testing frequently used on stainless welds in those plants, see penetrant testing in food and pharmaceutical plants.

Getting to an AWS Part B site from Minnesota

AWS divides the exam so that two of the three parts can be taken close to home. Fundamentals (150 questions) and Code Book (50 to 65 questions, open book) are computer-based tests delivered by Prometric in proctored centers; you schedule them once your AWS confirmation letter arrives with an eligibility code. The Practical part, 46 questions built around hands-on tasks with AWS-supplied equipment, is different: AWS gives it only at its seminar locations, on fixed dates.

The November 2026 AWS list of seminar and examination sites has no location in Minnesota. The closest listed sites for a Twin Cities candidate are Milwaukee and Chicago, with Indianapolis and Detroit further afield. That has practical consequences. Apply early, because the US deadline falls about six weeks ahead of the Part B date; wait for the confirmation letter before booking travel, as AWS advises; and plan the trip around a date when your employer can spare you. A minimum of 72 percent is needed on each part, and Part B is the one candidates from production shops most often underestimate. For neighboring markets, see CWI exam prep in Milwaukee and CWI exam prep in Chicago.

Where Twin Cities welders train, and the AWS Northwest Section

The metro has several public colleges that teach welding. Hennepin Technical College in Brooklyn Park, Saint Paul College, Anoka Technical College and Dunwoody College of Technology in Minneapolis all appear in listings of area welding schools; check each college's current catalog for program details. Formal welding coursework helps twice: it builds the skills the job needs, and trade or vocational courses count on the AWS eligibility table, reducing the experience a candidate must show compared with a high school diploma alone.

The local chapter of the American Welding Society for the Twin Cities is the AWS Northwest Section, part of District 15. It holds meetings and facility tours in the metro area, such as a recent plant tour in Chaska. Section events are a good place to ask which code books local employers prefer, find a study partner for the same Part B date, and meet the supervisors and inspectors who can later confirm your experience on an AWS application.

A six-day plan that fits a Minnesota work year

Construction here runs hard from spring to late fall, and outdoor work slows when the deep cold arrives. Many Twin Cities candidates therefore prepare in winter and sit Part B in spring before the season peaks. The course is built to allow that. Its six blocks run in a fixed order: fundamentals of processes, terminology, joints and symbols; metallurgy, testing, discontinuities, safety and inspector duties; practical skills for Part B; working inside your chosen code book for Part C; timed practice papers for all three parts; and a final day of weak-area review, exam strategy and an application documents check. A day-by-day breakdown lives on the national CWI preparation page.

Studying online, you get the study plan, course materials, original practice questions and instructor support by message, and you set the pace around your shifts. None of the practice questions comes from a real AWS exam. For a manufacturer or contractor preparing several people, the six days can run at your facility, and the practical day uses your gauges and your production weldments, so inspectors practice on the joints they accept every week. Atlantis has offices in Houston and Hyderabad; for on-site delivery the instructor travels to you.

Between study sessions, candidates who want to sharpen visual inspection judgment can use the Practical NDT welding workshop simulator, and the NDT practice tests are useful for anyone also working toward ASNT method qualifications.

Before you apply: eligibility, vision and documents

Three things are entirely between you and AWS. First, eligibility: the AWS table sets the years of welding-related experience you need according to your education, from a single year for a welding engineering or welding technology bachelor's degree up to twelve years for someone with less than eighth-grade schooling, with five years the common case for a high school graduate. Second, vision: every candidate must pass the AWS vision test. Third, the application itself, with education evidence, experience verification and your Part C code choice.

If you are short of the CWI experience requirement, AWS also offers the Certified Associate Welding Inspector (CAWI) credential, which has lower thresholds. A full explanation of the CWI requirements is in this requirements guide, and AWS's current examination and seminar fees are published on aws.org; the exam budget planner helps you add up travel to a Part B site as well.

Ask for a Minneapolis CWI prep quote

Send a short note covering who needs preparation, how many people, each person's likely Part C code book, the season you hope to sit Part B, and for employers, where the six days would take place. We reply within one business day. Start your Minneapolis enquiry here.

Some inspectors in the region also need NDT qualifications to perform tests themselves rather than ordering them. Atlantis trains to ASNT SNT-TC-1A, where your employer certifies you under its written practice; see NDT training in Minneapolis and visual testing in Minneapolis. Candidates further south can read about CWI exam prep in Kansas City.

faq.q: Is there an AWS Part B exam site in Minnesota?
faq.a: Not on the AWS list as of November 2026. Twin Cities candidates usually look at Milwaukee or Chicago for the practical part. Confirm current sites and dates on aws.org before booking anything.

faq.q: Can I take Parts A and C without leaving the Twin Cities?
faq.a: Parts A and C are computer-based tests given by Prometric at proctored centers across the country. Use Prometric's locator to find a center you can reach once AWS sends your eligibility code.

faq.q: Is the course delivered in a Minneapolis classroom?
faq.a: No. Atlantis keeps offices in two cities, Houston and Hyderabad, and none in Minnesota. You study online, or the six days can be brought to a Minnesota employer's site for its staff.

faq.q: Which code book should a MnDOT bridge inspector choose?
faq.a: AWS D1.5, the Bridge Welding Code, is the usual choice for steel bridge work. AWS offers the 2020 edition for Part C.

faq.q: Does cold-weather welding come up on the CWI exam?
faq.a: Not as a Minnesota topic, but the metallurgy behind it does: preheat, hydrogen cracking, cooling rate and impact toughness are all part of the Fundamentals content.

faq.q: Can a Twin Cities manufacturer have the six days at its plant?
faq.a: Yes. An employer can have the course run at its own facility for a group, and the practical day can use the plant's gauges and production weldments. Request a quote.

faq.q: Will Atlantis certify me as a CWI after the course?
faq.a: No. Only AWS can do that. The credential follows from meeting AWS eligibility, passing its vision test and scoring at least 72 percent on each of the three exam parts.

faq.q: Are the practice questions from past AWS exams?
faq.a: No. Each one is original, drafted around the topic list AWS publishes, and nobody at Atlantis ever sees an AWS examination paper.

faq.q: Is a CWI useful for refinery turnaround work in Minnesota?
faq.a: Often, yes, especially with ASME B31.3 as the Part C code. API inspector roles are separate credentials with their own exams, which Atlantis does not prepare candidates for.

faq.q: Where can I meet other welding inspectors locally?
faq.a: The AWS Northwest Section, part of District 15, holds meetings and facility tours in the Twin Cities area.
